title: In Good Company
full_review:
A sales executive at a sports magazine finds himself reporting to a man half his age in writer/director Paul Weitz's comedy-drama "In Good Company" (Universal), a mostly sharp and perceptive take on the heartlessness of today's corporate world.

Dan Foreman (Dennis Quaid) has been head of advertising sales for Sports America magazine for years, but he learns that Waterman Publishing has been taken over by Globecom, run by ruthless Teddy K (Malcolm McDowell).

Carter Duryea (Topher Grace), a Globecom cell phone sales exec, is brought in to replace Dan, and the latter has to endure both the indignity of reporting to a man with no experience in the field and the loss of his plush office.

Carter's first meeting with the staff threatens to be a disaster, but after a bumbling start, he hits his stride, and gives a rousing speech on the subject of "synergy" (the film's original title, by the way).

Despite pressure to fire Dan by Carter's superior, the smarmy Steckle (Clark Gregg in an appropriately hateful characterization), Carter keeps Dan on but insists Dan streamline the department by letting other old-timers on the staff go. Dan looks at his colleagues as family and resents Carter's bottom-line approach, but relents.

Carter's wife of six months leaves him, making Carter realize the emptiness of his life. One night when no one will have dinner with him, he invites himself over for dinner at Dan's home, where Dan's newly pregnant wife and daughters (including Scarlett Johansson as Alex) greet him with bemused wonderment.

On both the professional and personal fronts, Dan is firmly rooted in the past, and Carter's fresh-blood approach helps broaden Dan's perspective. Similarly, Carter comes to respect Dan's expertise, so each learns from the other, adding to the film's synergy theme.
A chance meeting at a street cafe brings Carter and Alex together, and they spend the day together, culminating in Alex asking Carter back to her NYU dorm room. She overcomes his hesitation by assuring him she's never done this before, and after creating a suitably romantic atmosphere in her little room by some hasty redecorating and playing appropriate music, they commence a sexual affair. (Moral considerations aside, that aspect of Weitz's script seemed dramatically flawed.)

Though Alex's actions will ultimately demonstrate to her father that she's no longer "Daddy's little girl," it seems peculiar that she -- even as embodied by the mature-beyond-her-years Johansson -- would actually sleep with Carter, despite his shyly boyish appeal. It is a brief misstep in an otherwise solid screenplay.
In any case, you know it's only a matter of time before Dan will discover what's going on, and when he does the results are indeed volcanic.

There are a couple of twists by the film's ending, which is more bittersweet than the conventional wrap-up you'd expect. Since both men come to the realization that they can learn something from the other, refreshingly, there isn't the obvious conclusion that everything "new" is "bad."

Quaid rarely gets the praise he deserves, and here, never making a false move, he delivers the goods as a totally convincing, square-jawed businessman. Grace is all callow opportunism tempered with youthful ambition and a basic decency. Seduction scene or not, Johansson gives another fine performance, nicely understated.
This is an intelligent, above-average comedy-drama worth seeing.

Because of some crude language, fleeting rear nudity and a permissive view of premarital sex, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
